text: You touch a hot pan. Before you even feel pain, your hand has already jumped away. How did your body decide so fast? Let's follow the message.
Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells, called neurons. Each one sends tiny electrical signals. Let's see how one neuron is built.
A neuron has three main parts. The dendrites receive messages. The cell body processes them. And the long axon carries the message away.
Many axons are wrapped in a fatty layer called myelin. It works like insulation on a wire, and makes signals travel much faster, up to about 120 meters per second.
At rest, a neuron is like a charged battery. There is more sodium outside the cell, and more potassium inside. The inside is slightly negative.
When enough input arrives, sodium channels open. Sodium rushes in, and the inside turns positive. That spike is the action potential. Then potassium flows out, and the cell resets.
The spike moves down the axon like a wave of falling dominoes. It is all or nothing. It either fires fully, or not at all.
At the end of the axon, the signal meets a tiny gap, called the synapse. The signal cannot jump across. Instead, the neuron releases chemical messengers, called neurotransmitters.
Neurotransmitters cross the gap and fit into receptors on the next cell, like a key in a lock. That passes the message on. Examples are dopamine, serotonin, and acetylcholine.

Now back to the hot pan. Pain nerves send the signal to your spinal cord. A reflex circuit there tells the muscle to pull back, before the message even reaches your brain. You move first, and feel it a moment later.
Remember three things: neurons use electrical spikes, synapses use chemicals, and myelin makes it fast. Next time, how does the spinal cord carry messages to your body?
